speechtext:

In view of the government's proposal to cut by half the number of libraries in Canada able to receive government publications free of charge, and in view of the fact that it will be citizens in the more remote parts of Canada who will pay for this measure by being deprived of access to information, at a time in the nation's history when we require greater, not less,
communication, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin):

speechtext:

In view of the fact that as of January 7 Air Canada will substantially reduce its services, especially on routes serving remote areas; in view of the fact that the same corporation says that it is compelled to make those changes as a result of the restricted number of authorized landings for pilots; considering that those reduced services added to other ones are reflected by higher transport costs, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette):

subsubtopic: POLICY RESPECTING COMMERCIAL ACTIVITIES OF FORMER HOLDERS OF FEDERAL PUBLIC OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister, perhaps I could direct my question to the Deputy Prime Minister who was the recipient of a letter from the Prime Minister dated October 18, 1976, setting out a reminder, as the Prime Minister called it, of the policy respecting commercial activities of former holders of federal public office in Canada.
Is the Deputy Prime Minister aware that the former minister of finance, Mr. John Turner, within weeks of leaving this House solicited various corporations with a view to offering them advice and guidance in respect of many matters pertaining to Ottawa, and succeeded in getting a group of ten to 12 to pay him $15,000 per annum for the advantage of his counsel? Is the House leader aware of this and, if so, does he feel it broke any understanding or guideline that existed at the time Mr. Turner left this House?

speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I am not aware of any such offer on the part of the former minister of finance, not following his career with the same interest as my hon. friend has done. Knowing the former minister of finance, I would conclude that he would conduct himself after he left office with the same degree of integrity that characterized his public service in the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: POLICY RESPECTING COMMERCIAL ACTIVITIES OF FORMER HOLDERS OF FEDERAL PUBLIC OFFICE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: POLICY RESPECTING COMMERCIAL ACTIVITIES OF FORMER HOLDERS OF FEDERAL PUBLIC OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, again I would direct my supplementary question to the House leader, who I know will recall that one of the principles set out in the October 18 letter addressed to him was the following:
Current and former holders of public office must ensure by their actions that there is no reasonable ground for belief that it is possible to have privileged access to government personnel or services.
Has the House leader had an opportunity to review the various memoranda and letters that have been sent out by the former minister of finance, in one of which he states:
As a starter, the chief executive officer should be put in as good a public policy posture as a cabinet minister.
Presumably he was referring to the chief executive officers of corporations.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: REQUESTED SPECIAL ECONOMIC PROGRAM FOR NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:

The consumer price index statistics released yesterday continue to indicate that the province of Newfoundland has the worst economic situation in the country. The city of St. John's showed the highest increase of all surveyed cities, with an
Oral Questions
astounding rate of inflation of 9.6 per cent over the past 12 months.
In view of the fact that the province has the highest inflation rate in the country, and that this becomes completely unacceptable when coupled with an intolerable level of unemployment, realistically, in the province, of approximately 25 per cent, will the minister accept the view that this is evidence enough to motivate him and the government to consider a special economic package for the province of Newfoundland as I have asked the minister repeatedly?

subsubtopic: REQUESTED SPECIAL ECONOMIC PROGRAM FOR NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as 1 said previously in reply to a question by the hon. member, most of the programs of the federal government are geared in order to help areas where there is slow growth, and in the last budget we made special provisions in the tax area in order to assist the developing areas of Canada to have a better break. subsubtopic: SALE OF NUCLEAR REACTOR TO TAIWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It follows on the question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Greenwood, in reply to which the minister said that the NRX research reactor in Taiwan has been under IAEA inspection ever since the ending of diplomatic relations between Canada and Taiwan.
Since it is my understanding that the United States took over international inspection following the break-off of diplomatic recognition between this country and Taiwan when Taiwan was no longer recognized by the UN, and since the agreement with the IAEA is no longer in force, would the minister say whether or not the Canadian government has made a new arrangement for the inspection of the nuclear research reactor in Taiwan to ensure that there is no opportunity for a recurrence of a situation such as developed in India with a similar research reactor?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: SALE OF NUCLEAR REACTOR TO TAIWAN
speechtext:
The hon. member will appreciate that, once again, as with all these complex questions, it is difficult to cover all the elements in an oral answer.
Yes, we have made some inquiries since the announcement of the weekend with regard to the change of status of the U.S.-Taiwan relationship and there has, indeed, been a report that the Taiwan assistant foreign minister has, in these last days, recalled that Taiwan is a party to the Non-Proliferation Treaty and has therefore pledged not to manufacture nuclear weapons. Another piece of information is that Taiwan ratified the NPT on January 27, 1970, and this reinforces the answer which I gave yesterday.
Obviously, the situation is changing to some degree and we do not have a definitive answer at the moment as to how, for example, IAEA safeguards will be supervised under the new arrangements, but as soon as I have that information I will be glad to pass it on to the House. I might conclude by saying that I think I understood the hon. member to say that it was not under IAEA safeguards. The information I have is that the IAEA safeguards are in place and are subject to IAEA inspections.

subsubtopic: SALE OF NUCLEAR REACTOR TO TAIWAN
speechtext:
I would like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether, when referring to the IAEA safeguards, he is telling the House that the IAEA agreement between that body and Taiwan is still in force. Is he giving the House that kind of information, because that is the important

assurance that would have to be sought and our information is to the contrary?

subsubtopic: MR. PETERS-INDIVIDUAL'S GRIEVANCE
speechtext: Order, please. I have a rather unique notice of a question of privilege from the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters). I am rather anxious to hear how he can relate this to anything to do with the procedures of the House.

subsubtopic: MR. PETERS-INDIVIDUAL'S GRIEVANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sent you notice under Section 17(2) of the standing orders of a question of privilege which, I believe, affects all members of this House. On several occasions I have raised a problem that confronts me as a member of parliament, and all other members, and have asked the House to do something about it. The problem is that one of our citizens is spending considerable time in front of the parliament buildings asking for relief from this institution.
I asked for advice, Mr. Speaker. I am given to understand that we have a privilege that goes back quite a way. It predates the Knowles parliamentary procedures and goes back to Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice, nineteenth edition.
This affects all members of the House. On several occasions we have made the request that this matter be handled in the House. The nineteenth edition of Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice, chapter IX, page 120, under the heading "Power of Both Houses to Secure Attendance of Persons on Matters of Privilege", has the following to say:
The House of Commons has the power to send for persons whose conduct has been brought before the House on a matter of privilege by an order for their attendance, without specifying in the order the object or the causes whereon their attendance is required (e); and in obedience to the order members attend in their places, and other persons at the Bar.
This came about a long time ago. It is indicated that the origin of a power which is judicial in nature is to be found, naturally, in the medieval conception of parliament as primari-

December 20, 1978
Privilege-Mr. Nystrom
ly a court of justice-the high court of parliament. We have often heard it said in this House that this is the high court of the country, that this is the last court, the court of last resort. It must, therefore, be a court of last resort for persons who wish to air a grievance or bring before parliament and the country something that they feel very strongly about when they are not in a position to petition in the normal sense.
As I am sure most other members of this House feel, I am a member of that court of last resort-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. PETERS-INDIVIDUAL'S GRIEVANCE
speechtext:
Order, please. If the hon. member is attempting to develop the thesis in some way that he ought to help someone redress their grievance by bringing them before the Bar of the House to air that grievance, I am sure he will understand that while he may have some substantive way to bring that about, it does not affect the privileges of the members of the House of Commons.
I have to be reasonable, and I have given the hon. member a few minutes to develop that question of privilege as we know it in the House in its classic definition. I think he will have to agree with me that while he has a very imaginative approach to try to help someone with their problem, I do not think there is any way he can fit it within the bounds of privilege as we know it.
I wish the hon. member the best of luck in trying to bring this forward under what other procedural grounds he may pursue.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is that, in view of the increased demand for more open government in Canada, it would facilitate the flow of confidential and nonconfidential information both within the public service and between the public service and the general public. Existing legislation places a specific responsibility on public servants at all levels to withhold any and all information that is marked "confidential". This bill makes a distinction between confidential and non-confidential information and job capacities, and implicitly requires the government to define more clearly the word "confidential" which is used liberally throughout the Revised Statutes of Canada.

speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) yesterday gave the Chair notice of his intention to raise, by point of order, the question of whether such a motion is able to deal with both the report stage and third reading of this bill in the way it has. I indicated to him I would examine the language of the Standing Order and the precedents. The language of Standing Order 75C does make specific reference to the inclusion of report stage and third reading, and it describes it specifically that way. I would, therefore, have some difficulty in interpreting that language in such a way as to prevent it from being done, particularly in view of the fact that a two-hour debate is provided during which the government may be freely criticized, as I am sure it will, for the use of the Standing Order. That is a separate question, as to whether it can be criticized or not, from the procedural right of the government to put the motion in this way. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I raised the matter yesterday you suggested it would be better if I were to do so today rather than yesterday, as I was prepared to do.
I realize that one rule which some persons follow in debate is never to admit thefe is any difficulty with your argument, but to insist that your case is watertight, ironclad, and all that. I am quite prepared to admit at the start that the wording in 75C does present some difficulty in respect of the point of order that I present for your consideration. However, I suggest there are times when what the House is about to do is so repugnant to the practices, precedents and traditions of this place that it should stop and take a look at it to see whether it is in order.
I said yesterday that if this motion were to cover two stages in a closure motion under 75C it would be the first time in the nine or ten years we have had this rule that it has been done. I have done some checking in the meantime. I have not read every page of Hansard and every page of the Journals back to

December 20, 1978
Allotment of Time for Bill C-14 1867, but I have done enough checking that I am in a position to say to Your Honour that if you do find you have to put this motion you will be the first Speaker in history to put before the House of Commons a motion for closure on a stage of debate that has not yet been reached.
We have had lots of motions for closure over the years. We have had House orders by agreements that were achieved before a debate started, but we have never had, by the use of the government's majority, a motion to set time limits on a debate before the debate at that stage had even been reached.
I point out that prior to 1913 there was no closure rule in the Standing Orders of the House Commons, but that in in 1913 we got such a rule. It was brought in by the Conservative government at that time, with the Liberals strongly opposing it. But, sir, even that rule which was brought in in 1913, about which I could say a good deal, had in it a provision that it was not to be used until there had been some debate on the stage in question.
That rule was badly abused by the Right Hon. C. D. Howe in 1956. There were times when some debate consisted only of a sentence or two. At any rate that is the tradition, the principle, and the spirit of closure in the Parliament of Canada. You do not use the government's majority to apply closure until there has been some debate. You do not anticipate the application of closure a day or two ahead, as this motion does in respect of the third reading of this bill.
As I say, we have a rule that limits debate to eight days on the throne speech before it starts, but that rule was agreed to, and we have a rule in respect of the budget debate being only six days after it starts. I have not been able to find any case where, by the use of the government's majority, a motion was passed before a debate started on a particular stage, prior to the one that is before us at this time. I feel this should be looked at very carefully before we proceed with it.
You may say to me, Mr. Speaker, that is good rhetoric, good philosophy, and so on, but then ask what we are going to do about the wording of the Standing Order. The wording that does present a problem, and I put that right on top of the table, is the phrase:
an allocation may be proposed in one motion to cover the proceedings at both the report and the third reading stages on a bill if that motion is consistent with the provisions of Standing Order 75(13).
Standing Order 75(13) is the order that says that third reading cannot be called on the same day on which the report stage was under debate. Therefore, it might be argued that in a sense there is consistency, although it seems to me there is a vagueness in Standing Order 75(13) that is not really covered by this provision.
May I point out that there are some things that are distinctive about Standing Order 75C as opposed to 75A and 75B, which tell us that about which we ought to be concerned. Neither 75A nor 75B requires any notice. They are motions that can be made by a minister without notice, because in the one case there is unanimous consent among parties, or in the other case there is majority consent. Standing Order 75B has never been used. I do not know whether we have used 75A as

such, but we have conformed to the spirit of 75A a number of times.
It is quite clear that when there is unanimous agreement or majority agreement you can do certain things that you cannot do when you are acting unilaterally under 75C. Standing Order 75C is distinct from the others in that it requires notice to have been given and, of course, that notice was given yesterday.
You will also note, sir, that there is nowhere in 75A or 75B any reference to proceedings that had already started. There is no requirement under 75A or 75B that the motion be put after the debate is under way. In other words, what the minister is trying to do in respect of the third reading stage could be done under 75A or 75B, but those are motions in respect of which there is either total agreement or majority agreement.
On the other hand, 75C makes a special point of the fact that an order under it is in respect of proceedings at the stage at which a public bill was then under consideration. In other words, if you are going to act under 75C, you are back to the traditions of a century of this parliament, namely, that you do not impose closure on something unless there has been some debate. That is there. I know there is the exception when we get down to it. However, there is also to be noted in all of this that it says there shall be only the one stage of a motion.
We then come to this exception. I have to admit that the words are clear. However, I submit that this rule has never been tested and that it in itself is inconsistent. On the one hand, it says there can be only one stage. It says there cannot be a motion respecting a stage on which there has yet been no debate. Then it turns around and says you can do the very things that the first part of the motion says cannot be done.
I went back to look at the origin of 75A, 75B and 75C. I have a pretty good memory of it, but I did not trust my memory. I had the feeling there was a report from the committee which brought in the rules in 1960 and that that report had some philosophizing in it that might be of help to me.
When I looked, I realized the case was that the rule changes that were debated in December, 1968, were brought before the House after reference to a committee. It was not today's standing committee but a special committee. The whole subject was referred to that special committee. It brought in a report with some philosophy and rationale in it.
The report had some nice things in it to the effect that although the government has to have certain powers to control the business of the House, there has to be co-operation. That was the philosophy behind what was rule 16A in the report that we debated in December, 1968. Rule 16A was withdrawn. That was part of the price for getting that report through.

As I say, my late friend C. D. Howe abused this very badly in 1956. The rule required that closure could not be used unless there had been debate. I remember very well when we got into committee and Mr. Howe stood up on the clauses of the bill. Clause 1 was called, he read out the marginal note and asked us to move on to clause 2. I emphasize that rule 75C did not have any committee consideration. It was a very contentious debate. The Liberals, much to their annoyance, were kept here all the month of July and finally had it put through under closure. Standing Order 75(13) protects the right of the House to insist that report stage and third reading not be taken on the same day. This motion is not repugnant to that clause and therefore I have to say that the motion is clearly within the terms of the Standing Order.
I wish to add just one other note. The hon. member spent a great deal of time on the subject of closure which, as he well knows, is covered by Standing Order 33 and which is, in fact, a motion to terminate debate at a stage on which the House must have launched itself. The fundamental difference between that Standing Order, which has been on the books much longer than this Order, is that this order is for time allocation which, in its fundamental terms, is a different exercise. Closure, of course, is an exercise terminating a debate which has already begun.
Time allocation has the fundamental difference of attempting to prescribe time for debate in advance, and obviously, in its very nature, has as part of it the ability of the House to program its time in advance, and in Standing Order 75A this is done by agreement. In Standing Order 75B it is done after a majority of the House leaders have agreed. In Standing Order 75C it can be done in a different way if these agreements have broken down. Now, whether the hon. member agrees with that or not, he can address himself to that subject in a few moments when the debate begins. But the language of the Standing Order has as its intention the advance programming of time, which is fundamentally different from closure as dealt with in Standing Order 33, and I certainly have to take this into account in examining whether the order is doing what it is intended to do.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to contribute a few words to the debate this afternoon. One of the underlying principles of this bill is to provide additional funding to the government for constructive job creation and training programs. This bill and other government funding would provide some $710 million for this purpose in the coming fiscal year, part of which would derive from the savings realized by the operation of the unemployment insurance program.
The opposition has explored this bill in great detail in committee. There were some 35 committee meetings, and all the amendments presented for consideration at report stage were dealt with in considerable detail at those meetings.
The opposition obviously has responsibility to oppose a bill and to make positive and constructive amendments to it, but there must come a time when members from all sides can vote. We can either have continued blockage or obstruction of a bill, or else it comes to a vote.
A motion under Standing Order 75C allows the government to set a time limit on debate, and provides that report stage and third reading can be dealt with in the same motion. In this case two sitting days have been proposed to deal with report stage and third reading. That would bring us up to two days before Christmas when I think many members will be getting away for the recess and all members will want to get back to their constituencies.
Allotment of Time for Bill C-14
As I recall, when changes were made to the rules in 1969, the idea was that the policy of a bill would be explored on second reading, it would be sent to committee for clause by clause study, then be dealt with at report stage and proceed for expeditious third reading. In the case before the House it is clear that the opposition, or at least the NDP, did not want to bring the bill to a vote but rather wanted to prolong discussion indefinitely. This bill would provide additional funding for direct employment programs and direct skill training programs and, surely, that is what most people in this country want. I receive many letters and communications, as I am sure other members do, asking why we spend so much money on welfare and unemployment insurance benefits and why we do not put people to work, and provide more training that would equip them for jobs.
This bill would make expanded job creation and training programs available to the government, Mr. Speaker. The program outlined by the minister at a cost of some $710 million for 1979-80 would do what many people want. It would provide 113,000 job-years of employment and activities, through such things as part-time jobs for students or on the job training in which 368,000 people could participate. This is a 70 per cent increase in work-years over previous figures.
I am especially interested in the fact that a lot of the emphasis is on youth employment, because often young persons coming out of high schools or post-secondary institutions cannot get jobs as they do not have experience on the job. They have not held jobs and have no letters of reference from previous employers. This program has a strong emphasis on youth with some $225 million for youth employment, some of which will come from savings through the UIC bill.
As a matter of fact, the job experience training program will be expanded from some 20,000 jobs to 63,000 jobs. This is for young people just coming directly out of school, and some $40 million will come from UIC benefits, creating a positive force for job training and job experience for young people, rather than being used as a direct pay-out from which we do not in the long term get any advantage for young people, such as experience on the job and becoming accustomed to being in the labour force. That does not occur when they are just drawing UIC benefits.
1 was also impressed by this job-creation program and the local economic development assistance program. We have in certain areas of the country local economic development corporations designed to seek out economic opportunities to create new businesses, but up until now there have been no equity funds available for this purpose. Often the banks are too tight-fisted, so there is no equity in the hands of the local entrepreneur who has a good idea and cannot put it together.
We have an economic development corporation in my constituency, and this program for local economic development assistance will provide some $10 million during the next fiscal year for the creation of about 1,000 permanent jobs.

I have always felt this indicates a lack of planning on the part of the government. If they had come up two months ago with this bill of prime importance to themselves, I assure you, Mr. Speaker, we would not now be discussing this motion. They brought in closure because they want to leave for Christmas. The bill is introduced in the last moment of the session, and we are expected to go through all stages in one or two days, when 90 per cent of Canadians are opposed to the bill. They want to force this down our throats. Some moments ago I heard another Liberal member say: "Finally, we can

collect $710 million at the expense of the unemployed." In order to create what? Only 113 man-years. And to get this, we are going to deprive 250,000 unemployed of something they are entitled to, unemployment insurance benefits for which they paid premiums. I suggest this is outright robbery. I said so yesterday and I say it again today. The people are cheated and are led to believe that it is in the interests of the country. It is as if to pay off municipal expenditures, Mr. Speaker, the mayor would decide to ask his fellow citizens to eat only one meal a day so as to make both ends meet. We need $117 million, one or two million within two years, so let us discontinue the payments. Premiums are collected, but let us drop the benefits. Let us keep that money for something else. However, the government knows quite well how to get the money to buy military toys worth $2.5 billion which have just been purchased as replacements for our planes. It is also ready to buy warships worth $1.5 billion while it is devoting $4 billion to save the party and try to give a new impetus to the economy. Some low income families living on the threshold of poverty will be deprived of their unemployment insurance. I say no. It is a shame. This government does not deserve to remain more than one day in power. How can they impose such nonsense on the people, Mr. Speaker?
How are the amounts collected? How has the number of inspectors been almost doubled now? Why? To make inquiries? Inquiries after one, two or three years to see if someone was eligible for unemployment insurance benefits four years ago? Mr. Speaker, in the six
years I have been in this House I have never been as saddened as I have been by the action of this government in imposing closure on Bill C-14, amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I am sad because of what the government and the minister, in particular, have done. The minister talks of the government's majority in this House. We are all well aware that the government has a majority, but surely we should move from the concept that might is right and use might for right. That would be a much better aspiration for this government when dealing with changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Right from the start of the bill I was closely associated with it on behalf of my party, and I saw not one iota or one scintilla of effort on the part of the minister or his government to be flexible, or even to entertain reasonable argument or propositions. The first thing we discovered when this bill was brought down-and through questioning witnesses who subsequently came before the committee-was that there was very little consultation with those who will be affected most, the workers of this country and the unions which represent them. There was very little consultation with the interested groups which will be affected by this bill, such as students and women. Even the government's own advisory group on the status of women was not consulted. We had the spectacle of the parliamentary secretary jamming the bill through committee. He limited the number of witnesses coming before the committee.
I come from an area where in October of 1977 the largest employers there, Inco and Falconbridge, announced a 3,000 person lay-off in the Sudbury basin. We fought like hell to get this government to keep people working, but this government was totally helpless. It could not provide jobs for people who wanted to work. The government rejected the stockpiling idea. It rejected an import duty on nickel coming from Argentina, the Philippines, and Australia. The government rejected those concepts, which would have kept 3,000 people working. Now we are witnessing the jamming through of a bill, clause 5 of which would reduce the benefits of those people who today are unemployed through no fault of their own. It would reduce their incomes from 66% per cent of average insurable weekly earnings to 60 per cent. The phonies to my right would have reduced those incomes to 50 per cent for those without dependants.

Just today I presented the minister with a list of about seven or eight people who found jobs in Thompson. They were laid off by Inco in Sudbury and found jobs in Thompson, but they have been unemployed, and they do not have the wherewithal to transport themselves to Thompson. Officials at the regional office of the minister's department in Sudbury said that they could not transport those workers to Thompson because there are unemployed people in Manitoba, particularly in Thompson, who must be hired first. I do not understand, and this is all so saddening to me.
I am a new Canadian, relatively speaking and it is sad to me that the government would propagate the concept that Canadian young people are lazy and that Canadian workers are lazy. I am sad that the government would legislate based on its perception of laziness. All reputable studies show that the puritan work ethic is alive and well in this country.
The party which forms the government has a long history of concern for society, but it has dragged itself to such a level that it must curry favour with the corporate sector so that it can get funds when the bagman goes around collecting for an election next spring. I am sad because the government has dragged itself to that level of expediency and concern about power. I am very sad about the performance of the government.
I have sat in committees of this House which have dealt with legislation dealing with corporations. It takes ten years to get a change in the Bank Act. That has been put off for the last couple of years. First we get a yellow paper, then a white paper, then a green paper, and then the subject matter, not a bill, is referred to a committee.
I sat in the committee which dealt with Bill C-16, the borrowers and depositors protection legislation. I saw every single financial institution and group come to the committee. Did the government jam that legislation through? Does it jam through legislation which affects the corporations of this country through? Oh, no, sir, it does not. But when it comes to workers' legislation such as changes to the unemployment insurance fund, they jam it through. I think that is sad because they have a double standard.
I cannot leave these phonies to my right alone because I recall the parliamentary secretary limiting the number of witnesses to nine, and pushing closure through the steering committee a week and a half ago. He was going to limit the debate to last Tuesday at eight o'clock. The Conservative member on the steering committee, the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke), agreed with the closure then, which subsequently resulted in the parliamentary secretary presenting a three point report from the steering committee. The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra turned around in the committee and, like the boa constrictor that this party has showed itself to be, he swallowed himself completely, twisting here and twisting there until he got to the eyeballs, then he regurgitated all over the committee. I thought it was a shameful display.

The Tories have an awful gall to come here and say they are opposed to closure when their representative was all for closure in the committee. The party to my right twisted here and twisted there. They have gutted themselves head on, as the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) would say. On the one hand they want to curry favour and curry votes in eastern Canada, and on the other hand they have the corporate sector and the John Bullocks of this society pushing them in the other direction. So they have had members speaking out of one side of their mouths and other members speaking out of the other side of their mouths. That is a totally shameful display.
The hon. member for LaSalle-Emard-Cote Saint-Paul (Mr. Campbell) said that this bill is all about abuse, that its purpose is to cut down abuse, when in reality the only provision in the bill which tends to punish abuse is the one dealing with employers, the provision which raises the fines on employers when they have broken the regulations by giving false information to the commission.
We have opposed the bill, and I make no apology for the role we play, because when it was fairly obvious that the minister was intransigent and the government's mind was made up, that the parliamentary secretary was the juggernaut in the committee trying to ram the bill through, it was at that point we decided that obviously the only thing to do was to try to stop the bill in its tracks. I say that, given the same circumstances, we would do that again.

The Progressive Conservatives agreed they wanted to see the bill go through the committee stage, and they agreed that with extra hours we could get it out of the committee on Tuesday night. Either they have no stamina or no guts, because when it came to the crunch they could not follow through on their promise and they reversed themselves completely. When it came to this stage, again we saw them trying to have their cake and eat it too.
Under the rules we have provision 75B where, with the agreement of the majority of the House, we can achieve a time allocation agreement. Here was an opportunity for the first time for the PC party to show its true colours. They said they would agree-although they did not quite agree with the bill as it was-to rule 75B and they would not force the government to use rule 75C. Here again they tried to have their cake and eat it too. We could bring in a new rule for the Tories, rule 75BC for those who want their cake and want to eat it too.

But we Liberals are not afraid. We have guts, we can take it. We will not let 17 members out of the 264, a mere 6.4 per cent of the elected members of parliament, stall and thwart parliament and stand in the way of the progress of this government. No, sir; we will take the action in a responsible way and use rule 75C because it will stop the filibuster attempted by the NDP. We have guts enough to do it, and we are doing it.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to the two speakers preceding me with interest. Perhaps I could deal with the last speaker first. I do not think I have heard such a bunch of crap since the speaker before him. Here he is accusing my party of being split on this bill. That is incredible. He tried to suggest that because the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) is concerned about the rather unfair measures in the act, and because the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) is concerned the provisions of the bill do not save enough money, that that indicates a split in our party. Not at all. What the heck! That is the essence of our proposal. We are all for restraint. We feel that the government is not saving money intelligently.
The manner in which the government is saving money will create tremendous hardship in the area east of the Ottawa river. The hon. member talked about a split. If he listened to any member of my party, surely it would be evident that two themes have been running through the contributions of every speaker. We are in favour of restraint.

subtopic: PROPOSED LIMITATION ON REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-14
speechtext: You have two teams, one on each side.

subtopic: PROPOSED LIMITATION ON REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-14
speechtext:
I was referring to themes, not teams. All of my colleagues have spoken in favour of our position. We have a united position.
Hon. members opposite, with the exception of the minister, who have spoken on the bill report stage, have spoken against it. When one talks about splits, surely there must be one opposite when all Liberal members do is attack the bill. In his opening remarks, the minister indicated that he wanted a constructive debate and that he wanted to listen to our position. He should listen to our position as other members of his party have done. They have become convinced by it.
This attempt to limit debate is not an attempt to limit my party so much, although we resent it. It is an attempt on the part of the minister to limit the members of his own party who are speaking out continuously against the bill. The minister indicated that he wanted to hear our positions brought out because he thought there would be some merit in debating them. The minister, several of his officials, and I, have had discussions. Some of our amendments were put forward after discussion with the minister. In a headlong rush to bring in the bill by January 1, the minister is going forward with a bill which he knows is inferior and which he knows will cause severe economic damage.

speechtext: The hon. member is misleading the House.

The minister is going forward with a bill which does not contain provisions that his officials feel are

The effects of this bill will create heardships in the area east of the Ottawa river. The government will be forced to alleviate them.
We have proposed two basic types of amendments which we wanted to discuss rationally. The first area of saving money should be an area where most Canadians feel abuse is centred. I am referring to people who quit their jobs for unjust cause. That should be the cornerstone. If one is looking to save money in a program, one must look at the areas of abuse. One cannot cut off people because they cannot find work when there is no work available. One goes after the people who are choosing not to work and choosing to collect.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: PROPOSED LIMITATION ON REPORT AND THIRD READING STAGES OF BILL C-14
speechtext:
The minister recognized this in discussions with his officials and myself. Our approach is a constructive one. It will save more money than the minister's approach. It will cause less hardship. It is interesting that not just members of the opposition support our approach and condemn the government's approach. It is not just the officials who feel we are on the right track. We have the Economic Council of Canada on our side as well.
Prior to the publication of the bill, the Economic Council of Canada conducted a review of the unemployment insurance situation. It warned against measures such as the repeater and new entrants ones which the government introduced. I should like to refer to the Economic Council of Canada discussion paper, which reads in part as follows:
A recent opinion poll showed that 60 per cent of Canadians felt that the minimum of eight qualifying weeks is too short and that eligibility based on 20 to 27 weeks would be more appropriate... A policy decision with respect to the minimum number of qualifying weeks should take into account the economic impact and abuses of the program. However, on equity and hardship grounds, the above popular belief cannot be supported ... it cannot be concluded that employees with less weeks of work have a higher expected relative cost ratio. The results of this paper ... indicate that employees with fewer weeks of work would, in the absence of unemployment insurance-
That is what the minister is talking about, cutting them off completely. It continues:
-be subjected to higher financial hardship. This finding should be taken into account when a political decision is made with respect to the minimum number of qualifying weeks.
This is a situation where a government-funded organization warned in advance of the bill against introducing the types of measures which the government introduced. The bill is a headlong rush to bring in anything which will reduce the deficit next year.
I understand why hon. members opposite are concerned about the size of the deficit next year. I understand why they feel that this is an area in which to save money. But it is evident to everyone who has attended the meetings and listened to the evidence that the government brought in ill-conceived and hastily conceived measures which will not do the job. These measures will do a tremendous amount of harm

around the country, which is why we feel we cannot support the bill.
Members of the government and committee members who attended the hearings looked at the impact of the bill. Many, many times the terrible effects of this bill have been brought forward, but I should like to bring them out once more. At the present time there is an unemployment rate of 8.3 per cent seasonally adjusted as of last month. There are only four provinces below the average rate of unemployment, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. The government's proposed measures will affect the provinces with low unemployment proportionately less severely than the provinces with high unemployment.
If one looks at the repeater and new entrants provisions, the proposed measures will affect 10 per cent of the unemployed in Newfoundland, 20 per cent in Prince Edward Island, 11 per cent in Nova Scotia, 12 per cent in New Brunswick, and 10 per cent in Quebec. In other words, the amendments will have maximum effect on areas with the highest rates of unemployment.
As several hon. members have pointed out, the 11.5 per cent relief rate for the repeater provision is a temporary salve. As the hon. member for St. John's East pointed out, Newfoundland and some of the other less-advantaged areas will be in terrible straits if they ever manage to bring down their unemployment rates below 11.5 per cent. As a result of the government's legislation and the new entrants and repeater provisions, if these areas manage to bring their unemployment rates below 11.5 per cent, the effects are just fantastic. Approximately 18 per cent of the unemployed in Newfoundland would be disqualified, 20 per cent in Prince Edward Island, 14 per cent in Nova Scotia, 19 per cent in New Brunswick, and 12 per cent in Quebec. The effect on the more prosperous areas is minimal, 6 per cent in Alberta and 8 per cent in Saskatchewan. Nearly one out of five to one out of six of the unemployed in less prosperous areas of the country will be affected by these provisions, and that is why we object to them.
We are proposing provisions which will eliminate abuse, spread the load fairly across the economy, and get at the abuse where it is likely to be concentrated, in the middle and upper middle class income families in central and western Canada. The government is going after money in any manner. Its proposals will affect one out of five to one out of six people in the Atlantic regions and in Quebec.
I see why the government wants to cut off debate. It is because the bill cannot stand up to scrutiny. Even hon. members opposite recognize that it is a bad piece of legislation. Repeatedly members across the way have spoken against it.

This bill is doing three things. First, it is cutting back benefits by 10 per cent. What possible relationship Could that have to the concept of abuse? That measure does not attack the abusers or cheaters but everybody, whether or not they are legitimately on unemployment. It is not a strict reading of the law, but a cut in the level of incomes of people who are unemployed. Canadians should understand that and it should be driven home to them.
